message.content:
I don’t have live access to real‑time air‑quality data, but you can quickly check the current status in Los Angeles using a few reliable resources:

| Source | How to use it | What you’ll see |
|--------|---------------|-----------------|
| **AirNow** (U.S. EPA) | Go to [airnow.gov](https://www.airnow.gov/), enter “Los Angeles” or your ZIP code. | Current AQI value, pollutant breakdown (PM₂.₅, PM₁₀, O₃, NO₂, CO, SO₂), and health‑advisory level. |
| **AQICN** (World Air Quality Index) | Visit [aqicn.org](https://aqicn.org/city/los-angeles/). | Live AQI, trend graph, forecast, and historical data. |
| **Local news apps** (e.g., LA Times, KABC) | Many local stations publish “Air Quality Alerts” on their websites or mobile apps. | Alerts for smog, wildfire smoke, or other events. |
| **Weather apps** (e.g., Weather.com, AccuWeather) | Look for the “Air Quality” section in the Los Angeles forecast. | General description (good, moderate, unhealthy) and pollutant levels. |

### Quick steps to get the current AQI

1. **Open AirNow** in your browser.  
2. In the search box, type “Los Angeles” or your specific ZIP code.  
3. Click the result for the nearest monitoring station.  
4. The page will display the **AQI** (0–500 scale) and the **primary pollutant** driving the index.

### Typical ranges for Los Angeles

| AQI Category | Description | Health advice |
|--------------|-------------|---------------|
| 0–50 (Good) | Clear, healthy | Normal outdoor activity. |
| 51–100 (Moderate) | Acceptable | Sensitive groups (children, elderly, people with respiratory issues) may want to reduce prolonged exertion. |
| 101–150 (Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups) | Some health effects | Sensitive groups should limit outdoor activities. |
| 151–200 (Unhealthy) | Everyone may experience health effects | Reduce outdoor exertion; consider indoor activities. |
| 201–300 (Very Unhealthy) | Serious health effects | Avoid outdoor activity. |
| 301–500 (Hazardous) | Extremely dangerous | Stay indoors, keep windows closed. |

If you’re planning to be outside, it’s a good idea to check the forecast for the next 24–48 hours as conditions can change rapidly, especially during wildfire season or after heavy rainfall when particulate matter can spike.

Feel free to let me know if you’d like help interpreting the numbers or understanding what each pollutant means!
